claims.statement: Resolved run GitHub tokens are held only in process memory under `(thread_id, principal)`, with normalized `login:`/`email:` principals isolating users and a separate bot principal; caching an unbound user token is refused.

User token cache entries expire at their token expiry with a 60-second skew or a hard 24-hour TTL; expired bot entries remain only until that cap so `resolve_thread_github_token` can re-mint them at the recorded repository scope rather than widening authority.

GitHub App installation tokens are minted by the App auth strategy and cached in process under a scope key containing installation ID, repository IDs/names, and permissions; a cached token is reused only until ten minutes before its GitHub expiry.

LangSmith sandbox proxy rules inject GitHub credentials as opaque Authorization headers for `api.github.com` and `github.com`, while the sandbox only receives `GH_TOKEN=proxy-injected`; refresh records and reuses the original repository and permission scope, and a near-expiry before-model refresh cannot broaden it.

The dashboard authenticates browsers through GitHub App OAuth and a HS256 `osw_session` JWT signed with `DASHBOARD_JWT_SECRET` for seven days; `require_session` rejects an absent or invalid cookie, binds the audit actor, and `/me` reports the identity with a newly evaluated admin flag.

The OAuth login/callback flow binds normal browser login to a nonce: `/auth/login` places its HMAC in signed state and the raw nonce in a cookie, and `/auth/callback` constant-time compares them before code exchange, identity lookup, login authorization, token persistence, and session issuance.

Post-login redirects are constrained by `sanitize_redirect_to`, which permits only non-protocol-relative relative paths or origins on the dashboard allowlist and blocks login/API paths, preventing attacker-origin redirects and callback loops.

Startup requires local auth, an allowed GitHub user, or an allowed GitHub organization; a login is authorized only by an exact allowed-user match or active membership in an allowed organization, whose GitHub App membership check uses `members: read` and fails closed on unavailable credentials, API failures, malformed responses, or inactive membership.

The dashboard router applies CSRF origin protection to all mutations: safe methods are exempt, while unsafe cookie-authenticated requests need an allowed Origin or Referer; a bearer-GitHub-token request without a session cookie is exempt because its credential is not ambient browser state.

Desktop login uses PKCE so no session is placed on the loopback redirect: after normal OAuth the browser receives a 120-second identity handoff code bound to the S256 challenge and fixed 127.0.0.1 callback, and redemption mints a session only after a constant-time verifier check; cloud-terminal tickets are separate 60-second JWTs bound to audience and thread_id.

GitHub webhook delivery is authenticated before payload processing by recomputing `sha256=HMAC(GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, body)` and constant-time comparing `X-Hub-Signature-256`; absent secret, missing signature, or mismatch is rejected.

Slack webhook routes validate the raw request before dispatch using an HMAC of `v0:timestamp:body`, constant-time comparison with the Slack signature, and a 300-second timestamp window; missing signing secret fails closed.
The Linear webhook route validates the raw-body HMAC-SHA256 from `Linear-Signature` before it parses or dispatches the payload, rejecting a signature failure.

The public `/webhooks/run-complete` route authenticates a query token against `RUN_COMPLETE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` with constant-time comparison and fails closed when the secret is unset, leaving run-failure replies disabled.

Persisted credentials are encrypted at rest with a MultiFernet built from `TOKEN_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, which accepts a most-recent-first key list so the first key encrypts and every key may decrypt; `decrypt_token` returns an empty string for invalid ciphertext or a missing key rather than raising.

When GitHub reports an unrecoverable refresh error (`bad_refresh_token` or `unauthorized_client`), the stored GitHub OAuth authorization is dropped unless a concurrent OAuth callback has replaced its refresh token, so callers require clean re-login rather than receive a known-stale token.

Admin identity is derived case-insensitively from `CONFIGURED_ADMINS` matches against email or GitHub login; dashboard dependencies evaluate the current session, while agent `require_admin` rechecks the current triggering actor or authorized schedule instead of trusting thread metadata.

Untrusted GitHub comment content is wrapped in reserved dangerous-external trust tags, while raw comments have those same reserved tags replaced before wrapping so an external author cannot spoof the trust boundary.

Dashboard origin enforcement is intentionally fail-open only when no dashboard origin is configured for local setups; otherwise unsafe cookie-authenticated requests require an allowed origin, and application startup enables credentialed CORS only for configured origins while rejecting wildcard origins.

Dashboard session cookies are HttpOnly; HTTPS split-origin deployments use Secure, SameSite=None cookies while same-origin or local HTTP uses SameSite=Lax, and the OAuth state cookie is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, auth-path scoped, and limited to the state TTL.

Personal credentials require metadata-confirmed private ownership: public threads always resolve workspace/App authority, while a private thread uses personal credentials only when the run actor equals its saved owner; unknown metadata, a system-private thread, missing owner, or a different actor fails rather than borrowing credentials.

PR credential selection prevents impersonation: a shared user-owned thread may name only a recorded participant as author, private threads are pinned to their owner, system threads use the App, and an ambiguous background completion must name a participant rather than act with saved user authority.

Per-user Notion credentials are stored under a login-specific namespace with encrypted tokens and secrets; status is redacted, lookup failure omits the integration tools rather than failing a run, and a reauthorization-required refresh deletes the connection.

Repository-scoped sandbox tokens are minted only for repository IDs reachable by the GitHub App installation; the installation-wide discovery token remains server-side and an unmatched requested repository grants no sandbox credential.
